{"basis":"measured","confidence":0.8,"fact_type":"defect","name":"ROOT CAUSE (walked, measured): a request whose Host is not allowlisted gets the MCP library's own "403 Forbidden: Host header is not allowed" (no content type, nothing naming --http-allow-host), and the server logs the library's "possible DNS rebinding attempt". reflow2's "say what would have worked" line prints once, at startup, on stderr. cap:remote-sessions set out to prevent exactly "an opaque 403 with nothing saying why", and put its answer only where the operator configures, never where the failure is met","source":"art:github-issue-616-oauth-resource-server","statement":"RUN AS THE SKILL (root-cause, fetched fresh), 2026-09-28, triaging art:github-issue-616-oauth-resource-server (Alex, GitHub issue #616, 2026-09-28, reflow2 0.70.0) under rule:field-feedback-issues-are-root-caused-and-ideas-are-brainstormed. Measured on 0.74.0.

① OBSERVED, the reporter's words: "--http-allow-host is mandatory behind any proxy, and its absence presents as a broken ingress rather than as a rejected Host header." EXPECTED: a refused Host is recognisable as a refused Host wherever it surfaces. NOT AFFECTED: loopback callers, and any caller once the flag names its host (ver:remote-sessions).

② PRECEDENT (search_design on the raw refusal text): cap:remote-sessions (verified) says the flag exists because "the failure mode it prevents is an opaque 403 with nothing saying why", and answers it with a warning when a non-loopback address is bound with no host named. main.rs names the rule: "Rule 4 — say what would have worked". No prior finding on the per-request reply.

③ CANDIDATES.
(A) The per-request refusal is opaque: its text and log come from the rmcp library, not from reflow2.
(B) No startup warning fires for a container bind, so nothing ever names the flag.
(C) An orchestrator turns the 403 into its own error before a person sees it: an HTTP readiness or liveness probe sends the pod's own address as Host, fails on 403, the pod never becomes ready, and the ingress answers with its own no-endpoint error. That really does look like a broken ingress.
(D) THE OBSERVATION IS WRONG: the 403 says Host plainly enough.

④ WHAT SEPARATES THEM. A predicts a body and log naming no reflow2 flag. B predicts silence at startup on --http 0.0.0.0. C needs a cluster. D predicts a body a proxy user would read as Host-related.

⑤ RESULTS (scratch server, --http 127.0.0.1:0; curl with `Host: reflow2.example.org`):
· POST /mcp, POST / and GET / all return `HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden`, body `Forbidden: Host header is not allowed`, with no content-type. The default Host gets 200.
· Server stderr, once per request: `WARN rmcp::transport::streamable_http_server::tower: rejected request with disallowed Host header (possible DNS rebinding attempt) host=NormalizedAuthority { host: "reflow2.example.org", port: None }`. Neither the body nor the log names --http-allow-host or the allowlist.
· --http 0.0.0.0:0, both single-design and --registry-root: startup prints "WARNING — bound to 0.0.0.0:…, which is reachable off this machine, but no --http-allow-host was given. Requests from another machine will be REFUSED with 403 … Pass --http-allow-host …". ⇒ B REFUTED: the right sentence exists, once, at startup.
· No route is exempt from the Host check: there is no health endpoint, and GET / is refused too. So an HTTP probe addressed to the pod gets 403. ⇒ C is CONSISTENT and NOT MEASURED (no cluster here).
⇒ A HOLDS. D is half-true: "Host header is not allowed" is accurate, but it names no fix and reads like a proxy or firewall policy.

⑥ CLASS: "say what would have worked" was applied at the moment of CONFIGURATION (a startup line on stderr, scrolled away in a container log) and not at the moment of FAILURE (the reply and the per-request log), because the failure is produced inside a dependency whose words reflow2 never replaced. The reply is the only text a person behind a proxy ever sees. The class is that the explanation lives where the operator looked once, not where the failure is met.

⑦ OUT OF SCOPE (no code changed). A test pinning the class: a request with an unlisted Host gets a reply whose body names the refused host, the allowlist, and `--http-allow-host`, and the server logs one line naming the flag. And a probe-shaped request (GET with the pod's own address as Host) either succeeds on a named health route or is refused with that same sentence. Size, as information: the rmcp layer produces the 403, so the fix is either reflow2's own Host check ahead of rmcp or a wrapper around it.

REPORTER'S CONCLUSIONS: HELD that it presents as something other than a rejected Host, at least in a proxy. QUALIFIED: reflow2's startup does name the flag, but only once, on stderr.

⑨ NOT ESTABLISHED: what Alex's ingress actually showed (a passed-through 403, or its own 502/503 after failed probes); whether his team's probes were HTTP or TCP.","subject_id":"cap:remote-sessions","valid_from":"2026-09-28"}
